title: CI/CD Pipeline Security

source_subtopics.title: Untrusted pull requests and build isolation

subtopics: Untrusted pull requests and build isolation
learning_outcomes: Explain the main security concern and trust boundary involved in CI/CD Pipeline Security.
Choose an appropriate defensive control for CI/CD Pipeline Security and state the assumptions under which it works.
Define a safe, reproducible verification step for CI/CD Pipeline Security, including a relevant negative or failure case.

content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 19: Software Supply Chain and Build Security. It builds practical understanding of CI/CD Pipeline Security with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: CI/CD Pipeline Security makes secure behavior repeatable across implementation, dependencies, configuration, and release. Apply least privilege and default-deny authorization on the server for each relevant action, object, and property, then test both allowed and denied cases.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: CI/CD Pipeline Security can be understood through this sequence: Inventory inputs → Limit build permissions → Verify artifact → Monitor advisories + drift. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 142.1 Pipeline identity and permissions; 142.2 Isolated build environments; 142.3 Protecting CI variables and secrets; 142.4 Artifact promotion and release controls; 142.5 Untrusted pull requests and build isolation; 142.6 Preventing unauthorized production deployments. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Apply least privilege and default-deny authorization on the server for each relevant action, object, and property, then test both allowed and denied cases.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.title: Safe reference example: CI/CD Pipeline Security
content_blocks.code:
name: security-checks
on:
  pull_request:
jobs:
  verify:
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - name: Run repository security checks
        run: python -m compileall -q app
content_blocks.expected_output: The job uses a minimal read permission and runs a local repository check on a pull request; production credentials are not exposed in this job.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Illustrative workflow fragment, not a complete hardened CI pipeline. Pin third-party actions to reviewed immutable versions, add secret/dependency scans, and protect deployment environments.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Apply least privilege and default-deny authorization on the server for each relevant action, object, and property, then test both allowed and denied cases. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “CI/CD Pipeline Security”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for CI/CD Pipeline Security in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
recap: CI/CD Pipeline Security is a security boundary/control topic, not a standalone checklist item.
Apply least privilege and default-deny authorization on the server for each relevant action, object, and property, then test both allowed and denied cases.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
